recent_posts.title: Vibe coding builds the mess, you still have to live in it – shipping bytes
recent_posts.summary: A critical reflection on vibe coding and AI-assisted development, arguing that while AI tools can generate code quickly, they accelerate 'cognitive debt' — the gap between a system's evolving structure and the team's shared understanding of it. Drawing on pieces by Robby Russell, Paul Stack, Margaret-Anne Storey, and Charity Majors, the author distinguishes between code that 'works' and code that 'stays working.' The core warning: when output is abundant, architecture becomes the scarce resource, and the friction that used to force developers to think before committing was doing invisible but essential work.

recent_posts.title: Does it work, or does it keep working? – shipping bytes
recent_posts.summary: The ongoing debate about AI-generated code persists because participants are answering different questions. One side asks 'does it work right now?' while the other asks 'does it keep working six months from now?' Both perspectives are valid but apply to different contexts. Disposable prototypes and throwaway code can be vibe-coded freely, while durable production systems require intentional architecture. The key decision developers need to make upfront is whether what they're building is disposable or durable — that framing resolves most of the debate.

recent_posts.title: How AI invalidates the heuristics experienced engineers rely on
recent_posts.summary: AI is disrupting the accumulated heuristics and rules of thumb that experienced engineers rely on. Drawing on Marc Brooker, Kent Beck, and others, the author reflects on how roughly 90% of current engineering skills may become obsolete while 10% — judgment, vision, managing complexity — become exponentially more valuable. The uncomfortable reality is that senior engineers carry miscalibrated priors they can't easily identify, while juniors may actually have an advantage because they haven't built up the wrong instincts. The author describes the personal challenge of distinguishing legitimate intuition from outdated muscle memory when working with AI tools.

recent_posts.title: Pragmatic early adopter meets coding agents
recent_posts.summary: A pragmatic developer shares early impressions of using coding agents, specifically the obra/superpowers toolkit combined with Claude. The main focus is on context management — how to point agents to the right code and teach them your personal development style. The author prefers a lightweight toolchain (Vim, TMUX) and finds obra/superpowers fits that philosophy better than heavier alternatives like 'get-shit-done'. Also notes Claude's new CLAUDE_CODE_NEW_INIT env var for making CLAUDE.md more dynamic as a promising direction.

recent_posts.title: How tool subscriptions shape a solo consultant's workflow and attention
recent_posts.summary: A freelance consultant reflects on how tool and service subscriptions affect not just finances but cognitive load, workflow alignment, and business focus. The post covers the hidden costs of SaaS fragmentation (especially Italian invoicing compliance), the tradeoffs of cloud providers like Hetzner vs hyperscalers, communication tool friction with Slack vs email, and a measured approach to LLMs and agentic coding. The core argument: every subscription is a commitment of attention, and attention is the real scarce resource for a solo consultant.

recent_posts.title: Full automation means fast rollbacks and proactive communication
recent_posts.summary: Full automation in DevOps means more than just automated deployments—it requires fast rollbacks, proactive communication, and processes that work under pressure. A 30-minute CI pipeline might be acceptable for releases but fails during outages when quick rollbacks to trusted versions are critical. Effective automation guides attention where it matters most, whether managing 4000 EC2 instances or 3 containers. The principles remain the same regardless of scale, though smaller environments allow faster iteration.

recent_posts.title: Buy vs build when it comes to dependency management
recent_posts.summary: Explores the evolution of developer perspectives on dependencies across career stages, from junior engineers wanting to learn by avoiding them, to mid-level developers embracing them for speed, to senior engineers being cautious about complexity. Compares software dependency decisions to manufacturing choices, arguing that both require careful cost-benefit analysis rather than blanket rules.

recent_posts.title: Why you don't always need single page applications and API first architecture
recent_posts.summary: A developer reflects on the complexity of single page applications and API-first architecture, arguing that these approaches aren't always necessary. The author suggests starting with simpler server-side solutions and adding APIs later when actually needed, rather than following industry trends from large tech companies that may not apply to smaller projects. The key message is to make technology decisions based on current needs and personal context rather than predetermined architectural patterns.

recent_posts.title: Stanford CS229 I Machine Learning I Building Large Language Models (LLMs)
recent_posts.summary: The post discusses the importance of learning about large language models (LLMs) and their impact on the environment. It highlights a Stanford CS229 presentation on YouTube that covers specialized training, transformation, and data quality in generative AI. The author emphasizes the ongoing effort to make these technologies more efficient and sustainable.

recent_posts.title: Traverse a SQL query to get what you like with Rust
recent_posts.summary: A developer shares their experience of parsing SQL queries to dynamically load tables in Apache Datafusion using Rust. They discuss their approach, using the sqlparser crate, to extract a list of tables from SQL queries to enable feature validation without fully implementing CatalogProvider and SchemaProvider. Sample Rust code and tests are provided to demonstrate the process.
